paragraphs: When different senses provide information about an event, the nervous system must decide whether those signals share a source. Combining them makes sense under a shared-source explanation; keeping them separate fits a different-source explanation. This paper treats that choice as Bayesian model selection and asks how neural circuits could perform the required comparison.

The proposed generative model represents information through populations of neurons and incorporates both the stimulus feature and its reliability. For circular quantities such as heading direction, the authors derive an analytical expression for the Bayes factor, which compares the evidence for the two explanations. Its geometric interpretation allows the computation to be implemented through simple additive operations on population codes.

Numerical simulations produce response patterns consistent with previously observed opposite neurons in visual-vestibular brain areas. That agreement supports a potential circuit mechanism for causal inference. The result connects a formally motivated computation with observed neural tuning, without establishing that the brain necessarily implements this particular model.
neurips-2019-a-normative-theory-for-caus.tldr: A Bayesian model shows how neural population codes could compute whether sensory signals come from a shared source.

paragraphs: Neural network certification uses mathematical approximations to establish properties of a network. The precision of those approximations matters: a loose representation can leave a verifier unable to establish a property. This paper focuses on convex relaxations of ReLU activations and the precision barrier created by treating each neuron separately.

The proposed framework, k-ReLU, approximates groups of ReLUs within a layer jointly. This lets the approximation retain relationships between the inputs of different neurons. Those dependencies are lost in the single-neuron triangle relaxation and its approximations. The parameter k specifies how many ReLUs are considered together, making the size of the joint treatment an explicit part of the framework.

The method can be incorporated into existing verifiers to improve their precision. Experiments report substantially more precise certification than the compared state-of-the-art systems while retaining scalability. The contribution is therefore both a richer mathematical approximation and a way to strengthen verification tools by accounting for interactions that independent neuron approximations discard.
neurips-2019-beyond-the-single-neuron-co.tldr: k-ReLU improves neural network certification by jointly approximating groups of neurons and preserving dependencies between them.

paragraphs: Decompilation tries to recover understandable high-level programs from binary executables. The paper identifies three difficulties with conventional tools: specialization to particular language pairs, failure to preserve program functionality, and outputs that are difficult to interpret. Coda approaches the task as a learned process that first constructs a candidate program and then repairs it.

Its first stage uses an encoder sensitive to instruction types and a tree decoder to generate an abstract syntax tree. Attention helps guide this initial code sketch. A second stage repeatedly corrects the sketch, using an ensemble of neural error predictors to guide the changes. The design separates approximate reconstruction from targeted error correction.

Across the reported benchmarks, Coda averages 82% program recovery accuracy on unseen binaries, compared with 0% for the evaluated state-of-the-art decompilers. The abstract also reports a 70% program-accuracy margin over an attention-based sequence-to-sequence model. These findings support the approach in the evaluated setting and highlight implications for both security analysis and software intellectual-property protection.
neurips-2019-coda-an-end-to-end-neural-p.tldr: Coda learns to recover programs from binaries by generating a structured code sketch and iteratively correcting predicted errors.

paragraphs: Risk measures estimated from data can differ from their population values. This paper studies how large those errors can be for conditional value-at-risk, or CVaR, and Cumulative Prospect Theory values. Its central strategy is to translate existing bounds on distributional estimation error, measured by Wasserstein distance, into bounds on errors in these risk measures.

For CVaR, the authors derive a two-sided concentration bound from an independent, identically distributed sample. It covers errors in both directions and can apply to unbounded random variables under the stated distributional assumptions. They also obtain specialized results for sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential variables, extending beyond earlier results restricted to bounded variables or one-sided errors.

For Cumulative Prospect Theory, the analysis covers bounded and sub-Gaussian variables. The resulting bounds match a known result in the bounded case and improve a known result in the sub-Gaussian case. A stochastic bandit algorithm that optimizes CVaR, together with its regret bound, demonstrates how these estimation guarantees can inform sequential decisions.
neurips-2019-concentration-of-risk-measu.tldr: Wasserstein concentration bounds yield stronger guarantees for estimating risk measures and support a CVaR-based bandit algorithm.

paragraphs: A selective classifier can decline to answer when it lacks confidence. Its objective is to predict well on the fraction of examples it accepts, called coverage. This paper makes abstention part of the learning problem by adding one output to an ordinary classifier: alongside the original classes, the network can choose to withhold a prediction.

The training loss comes from portfolio theory and the doubling rate of gambling. Predicting a class corresponds to betting on an outcome, while abstaining corresponds to keeping some winnings in reserve. Optimizing this objective trains the network to balance committing to an answer against retaining that reserve, making the treatment of low confidence part of end-to-end learning.

The approach requires almost no changes to the model architecture or inference procedure beyond those involved in its formulation. Experiments on SVHN and CIFAR10 show that it can identify uncertain data points and achieve strong selective-classification results at multiple coverage levels. The findings support learning when to answer alongside learning what answer to give.
neurips-2019-deep-gamblers-learning-to-a.tldr: A gambling-inspired loss teaches classifiers to balance making predictions with abstaining when confidence is low.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning uses posterior inference to reason about unknown model quantities from data. When those data describe people, the inference procedure may also need formal privacy protections. This paper extends differentially private Bayesian learning with a general Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that applies to posterior inference in arbitrary models.

The central contribution concerns the privacy of the sampling procedure's accept-or-reject decision. The authors decompose the Barker acceptance test in a way that makes this decision's Rényi differential privacy cost possible to evaluate. This provides a basis for privacy accounting without relying on the unrealistic assumptions about Markov chain convergence that the paper identifies in earlier approaches.

The authors additionally show how data subsampling and approximate acceptance tests can strengthen the differential privacy guarantee. These results broaden the applicability of private posterior inference by addressing privacy within the sampling mechanism itself. The stated advance is a general algorithm and its privacy analysis; the convergence-related claim concerns the assumptions required for that privacy guarantee.
neurips-2019-differentially-private-mark.tldr: A general private MCMC algorithm accounts for accept-or-reject privacy costs without unrealistic assumptions about chain convergence.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest-neighbor search finds points close to a query without exhaustively comparing every candidate. Keeping a large search index in main memory can make this expensive. DiskANN uses a graph-based index and an SSD to index, store, and search a billion points on one workstation with 64GB of RAM.

The system targets three goals together: accurate retrieval, low latency, and many indexed points per machine. On SIFT1B, the reported configuration handles more than 5,000 queries per second with mean latency below three milliseconds and over 95% 1-recall@1 on a 16-core machine. Compared methods with similar memory footprints reach roughly 50% on that recall measure.

At high recall, the abstract reports support for five to ten times as many points per node as the compared graph methods. DiskANN also introduces Vamana, a graph index described as more versatile even for in-memory use. The findings demonstrate that SSD-based search can achieve the three goals together in the evaluated billion-point setting.
neurips-2019-diskann-fast-accurate-billi.tldr: DiskANN combines graph indexing with SSD storage to deliver fast, high-recall billion-point search on a single workstation.

paragraphs: In some classification problems, a decision determines whether its true outcome ever becomes visible. A lender observes repayment only after granting a loan, for example. This paper studies a sequential version of that problem: individuals arrive from a fixed but unknown distribution, receive a positive or negative classification, and reveal their labels only after positive decisions.

The algorithm must satisfy statistical fairness constraints at every round with respect to the underlying distribution. These include constraints involving equal false-positive or false-negative rates. The challenge is therefore to improve decisions while learning from selectively observed labels and maintaining the specified fairness condition throughout the process.

The authors derive upper and lower bounds on the regret cost of these constraints and characterize that cost as mild. They also provide an oracle-efficient algorithm attaining the upper bound. Together, the bounds describe the learning price of requiring fairness continuously, while the algorithm establishes that the stated upper rate is achievable within this fixed-distribution, partial-feedback formulation.
neurips-2019-equal-opportunity-in-online.tldr: The paper characterizes the regret cost of maintaining statistical fairness when only positive classifications reveal their true labels.

paragraphs: A neural network can exceed the memory available on a single accelerator even when increasing its capacity would improve quality. This paper presents a pipeline-parallel library, called TensorPipe in the supplied abstract, for networks expressible as sequences of layers. Its purpose is to make large-model training transferable across tasks and architectures.

The method assigns successive groups of layers to separate accelerators. A batch-splitting pipeline algorithm then organizes work across those groups, allowing different parts of the network to run on different devices. The abstract reports almost linear speedup as a model is partitioned across multiple accelerators, addressing both capacity and training efficiency.

The demonstrations cover image classification and multilingual translation. A 557-million-parameter AmoebaNet reaches 84.4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-2012. A single six-billion-parameter, 128-layer Transformer trained on over 100 languages achieves better quality than all bilingual models in the reported comparison. These examples show the approach supporting large networks with distinct architectures under the common requirement of a layered sequence.
neurips-2019-gpipe-efficient-training-of.tldr: Pipeline parallelism and batch splitting enable efficient training of very large layered networks across multiple accelerators.

paragraphs: Forecasting many related time series requires modeling how their observations depend on one another. Allowing those relationships to change over time makes the problem harder, particularly when a covariance matrix must describe thousands of series. The paper addresses the computational and numerical burden that can restrict existing methods to much smaller collections.

The proposed model combines a recurrent neural network for time series with a Gaussian copula process output model. A low-rank covariance structure reduces the number of parameters used to represent dependencies. The copula formulation also accommodates non-Gaussian marginal distributions, so individual series need not each follow a Gaussian distribution.

Together, these choices make it possible to model changing correlations among thousands of series with substantially reduced computational complexity. Experiments on several real-world datasets show significant accuracy improvements over the compared state-of-the-art baselines. An ablation study examines the contributions of individual components. The results support combining temporal modeling, flexible marginal distributions, and a compact dependence representation within one forecasting system.
neurips-2019-high-dimensional-multivaria.tldr: A recurrent forecasting model with a low-rank Gaussian copula represents changing dependencies among thousands of non-Gaussian time series.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a system can answer logical queries when some background knowledge is written as formulas and some is available only through examples. The examples are independently drawn from a fixed distribution. The goal is to combine formal reasoning with learning while retaining a rigorous account of what the answers mean.

The approach builds on PAC semantics, which supports a probabilistic form of reasoning weaker than classical entailment while requiring few assumptions about the distribution. Earlier robust approaches were largely restricted to essentially propositional languages with finitely many atoms. The paper develops a theoretical approach for universally quantified first-order clauses over a countably infinite domain.

The key ingredient is symmetry among constants in the logical language. Exploiting those symmetries lets the authors extend implicit learnability and compute queries against background knowledge learned implicitly from examples. The contribution is a route beyond the finite propositional setting for the specified class of formulas, linking relational reasoning to sample-based knowledge without requiring all learned knowledge to be represented explicitly.
neurips-2019-implicitly-learning-to-reas.tldr: A symmetry-based theoretical approach extends implicit learning and query answering to first-order clauses over a countably infinite domain.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter provides a way to average probability measures using optimal transport geometry. Computing it can become prohibitively expensive as the measures have more support points. This paper revisits interior-point methods, a traditional second-order optimization approach, and asks whether their computational burden can be reduced by exploiting the specific structure of this problem.

The authors develop an adapted interior-point method that uses the special matrix structure arising in barycenter computation. This reduces iteration complexity and accelerates the Newton procedure inside the optimizer. The main idea is to organize the second-order computation around the problem's structure, making an otherwise costly class of methods more practical.

Numerical comparisons across various distributions demonstrate computational advantages over existing algorithms and a balanced tradeoff between speed and accuracy. Applications to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST image benchmarks further demonstrate practicality. The stated findings support the adapted solver as an effective approach to Wasserstein barycenters, with its benefit coming from specialized optimization rather than the regularization approaches discussed in the abstract.
neurips-2019-interior-point-methods-stri.tldr: Exploiting the Wasserstein barycenter problem's matrix structure makes an adapted interior-point solver faster while balancing accuracy and speed.

paragraphs: Long tasks can be easier to learn when an agent can combine reusable sub-skills. Hierarchical reinforcement learning seeks such a decomposition, but choosing useful abstractions remains difficult. This paper proposes language as the interface between levels, motivated by its ability to combine familiar elements into structured instructions for different tasks.

The approach learns a low-level policy that follows instructions and a high-level policy that reuses language abstractions across tasks. To study this compositional learning, the authors introduce an open-source object-interaction environment built with the MuJoCo physics engine and CLEVR engine. The environment supports tasks requiring sequences of coordinated interactions with objects.

Agents learn diverse extended behaviors, including object sorting and rearranging multiple objects, with some tasks learned from raw pixels. The analysis compares language with non-compositional abstractions receiving the same supervision and finds language's compositional structure critical for learning and systematic sub-skill generalization. These findings support structured language as a reusable organizing mechanism for the evaluated hierarchical learning problems.
neurips-2019-language-as-an-abstraction-.tldr: Language-based instructions connect reusable sub-skills to high-level policies, supporting extended tasks and compositional generalization.

paragraphs: Mapping structural brain connectivity from diffusion-weighted MRI typically involves expert analysis and rule-based models. This paper explores a data-driven framework for automatically extracting an individual's connectome. Its aim is to fit the measured diffusion information while favoring structures that are biologically plausible.

The framework uses a tensor encoding and an objective with group regularization to encourage plausible fascicles, or bundles of fibers. The authors show that the objective is convex and has a unique solution, giving identifiability within the proposed formulation. This mathematical property makes the inferred solution well defined for an individual under the model.

Because the sparse optimization problem is extremely high dimensional, the authors design a specialized greedy algorithm to reduce the number of parameters. It significantly improves on Orthogonal Matching Pursuit in the reported comparison. Analysis of the resulting solutions shows accurate reconstruction of diffusion information alongside contiguous fascicles with smooth directional changes. These findings connect computational tractability, a unique optimization solution, and the structural preferences built into the objective.
neurips-2019-learning-macroscopic-brain-.tldr: A convex, group-regularized framework learns individual brain connectomes while encouraging contiguous fascicles with smooth directional changes.

paragraphs: Neural networks can predict how a system's state changes over time, but predictive ability alone does not establish mathematical properties of the learned dynamics. This paper focuses on stability. It proposes a learning approach that guarantees stability across the entire state space, making a formal property part of model construction.

The method jointly learns the dynamics and a Lyapunov function. That function supplies the measure under which the dynamics are guaranteed to be non-expansive. Learning both components connects the predicted evolution to a mathematical certificate, so the stability statement is expressed in terms of the learned Lyapunov function.

The authors show that these systems can model simple dynamical processes. They also combine the approach with deep generative models to learn more complex dynamics, including video textures, through end-to-end training. These demonstrations indicate that imposing the stated stability property can coexist with learning useful dynamics. The guarantee concerns stability of the learned system, while the examples establish its ability to represent the processes considered.
neurips-2019-learning-stable-deep-dynami.tldr: Jointly learning dynamics and a Lyapunov function gives neural dynamics models a stability guarantee across the entire state space.

paragraphs: A shared team reward can make it difficult for cooperating agents to learn different, useful behaviors. Each agent needs guidance about its own actions, even though success is measured collectively. LIIR addresses this problem by learning a separate intrinsic reward function for each agent in decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning.

An agent's intrinsic reward contributes to a distinct proxy critic, which guides updates to that agent's policy. The intrinsic reward function is itself trained toward maximizing accumulated environmental team reward. This links individualized learning signals to the original cooperative objective, combining ideas from reward shaping and methods that assign credit through critics.

The authors compare LIIR with several state-of-the-art multi-agent methods on StarCraft II battle games. The results demonstrate its effectiveness in those tasks and show that it can provide informative rewards to individual agents at each time step. The contribution is a learned mechanism for differentiating agents' training signals while keeping the optimization of those signals aligned with team-level success.
neurips-2019-liir-learning-individual-in.tldr: LIIR learns agent-specific intrinsic rewards that guide individual policies while being optimized for the team's shared objective.

paragraphs: A bandit learner must explore actions to discover their value, but exploration is difficult when safety also depends on unknown parameters. This paper formulates a linear stochastic bandit problem with a safety constraint that depends linearly on an unknown vector. The learner must act conservatively to satisfy that constraint at every round with high probability.

Safe-LUCB adapts an upper-confidence-bound approach through two phases. First, it samples randomly from a restricted set of known safe actions to learn an approximation of the larger safe set. It then balances exploration and exploitation while gradually expanding its estimate of which actions are safe and controlling regret.

The analysis gives both a general regret bound and a problem-dependent bound tied to the optimal action's location within the safe set. That connection shows how the geometry of the safe choices enters the learning guarantee. The authors also propose a modified heuristic informed by this analysis to improve regret, linking the theoretical characterization to an algorithmic adjustment.
neurips-2019-linear-stochastic-bandits-u.tldr: Safe-LUCB learns unknown linear safety constraints while balancing reward-seeking exploration with high-probability safety at every round.

paragraphs: Setting prices for many products is challenging when demand changes and products influence one another's sales. This paper studies an evolving demand model whose cross-elasticities have low-rank structure based on fixed, hidden product features. Under that assumption, a pricing problem with many products can be approached through a much smaller underlying feature space.

The authors reduce revenue maximization to online bandit convex optimization, using observed demands as additional information. Their algorithms choose prices through optimization in the low-dimensional span of the latent features. They simultaneously learn that span through online singular value decomposition of a specially constructed matrix of demand observations.

The resulting revenue approaches that of the best fixed price vector chosen in hindsight. The stated convergence rate depends on the demand model's intrinsic rank rather than the number of products. This makes the structural assumption central to the result: a large catalog can admit a lower-dimensional learning problem when its changing demand relationships are governed by fixed latent features.
neurips-2019-low-rank-bandit-methods-for.tldr: Under a low-rank demand assumption, dynamic pricing algorithms achieve revenue guarantees governed by latent dimension rather than product count.

paragraphs: A regression design matrix formed as a Kronecker product can be enormous even when its component matrices are manageable. This paper develops faster algorithms for approximating regression solutions without explicitly forming that expanded matrix. It considers residual norms with p between one and two, including ordinary least-squares regression.

For p equal to two, the stated running time depends on the total number of nonzero entries in the factor matrices, with no dependence on the number of nonzero entries in the response vector. For p below two, the running time also includes the response vector's nonzero entries. These improve the corresponding earlier bounds described in the abstract.

The authors also study regression over all pairwise differences of input rows, giving an algorithm whose stated running time depends on the original matrix's nonzero entries and avoids constructing the quadratic-size expansion. Related Kronecker low-rank approximation algorithms likewise work at the scale of the factors. The common contribution is computation that exploits structured inputs without paying to materialize their much larger expansions.
neurips-2019-optimal-sketching-for-krone.tldr: New algorithms accelerate Kronecker-product regression and related approximation problems by avoiding explicit construction of expanded matrices.

paragraphs: Knockoff filters control false discoveries when selecting variables, but that protection leaves a separate question: how many real signals can they recover? This paper studies their power when predictors are correlated. It moves beyond the independent Gaussian setting to examine how a general covariance structure affects consistency.

The authors introduce effective signal deficiency, a functional of the predictors' covariance matrix that predicts consistency for several variable-selection methods. The analysis highlights the precision matrix and the associated conditional-independence structure. This identifies properties of predictor dependence that matter for recovering signals while driving false discoveries toward zero in the consistency regime.

Building on that connection, the paper proposes Conditional Independence knockoff. The procedure is defined for Gaussian tree graphical models or sufficiently sparse graphs and can compete with more sophisticated knockoff filters. Synthetic-data experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution links power analysis to dependence structure and uses that link to motivate a simpler procedure under the stated graphical conditions.
neurips-2019-power-analysis-of-knockoff-.tldr: Effective signal deficiency links variable-selection consistency to predictor dependence and motivates a conditional-independence knockoff procedure.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from observational data requires evaluating decisions without collecting new outcomes under that policy. This paper addresses continuous actions when the policy that generated the data is unknown and must also be estimated. Its model assumes a known parametric form for the value function's dependence on treatment while leaving its dependence on observed contexts unspecified.

The authors construct a doubly robust off-policy value estimate and use it for policy optimization. They establish robustness to estimation errors in the policy function or regression model, as well as a variance result attaining the semiparametric efficiency bound. These findings address both sensitivity to estimated components and the statistical efficiency of evaluation.

When the true value function falls outside the assumed form, the results also apply with regret measured against its best projection into that functional space. This changes the reference used to assess performance under misspecification. A synthetic personalized-pricing example evaluates the method experimentally, illustrating the extension of observational policy learning from discrete to continuous actions.
neurips-2019-semi-parametric-efficient-p.tldr: A doubly robust, semiparametrically efficient estimator supports policy learning with continuous actions from observational data.

paragraphs: This paper studies deep networks with piecewise affine, convex nonlinearities through the geometry of their input spaces. Their layers can be represented as max-affine spline operators: each layer partitions its input into regions and applies a different affine mapping within each region. The question is how those regions are organized and change across layers.

The authors show that a layer's partition corresponds to a power diagram, an extension of a Voronoi tiling. The number of regions grows exponentially with the number of neurons. Composing layers produces progressive subdivisions, for which the paper gives an analytical form. These subdivisions also constrain the affine maps, reducing their complexity despite the potentially enormous number of regions.

For classification, the analysis yields a formula for the network's decision boundary and a curvature measure depending on its nonlinearities, weights, and architecture. Numerical experiments support and extend the theoretical results. The contribution connects layer composition to an explicit geometric description of both internal partitions and the resulting classification boundary.
neurips-2019-the-geometry-of-deep-networ.tldr: For a specified class of networks, power-diagram subdivisions describe layer geometry, constrain local mappings, and characterize decision boundaries.

paragraphs: Boosting variational inference approximates a difficult probability density by adding simple distributions to a mixture one at a time. Existing guarantees can require conditions that fail in practice, leading to degenerate component optimizations. This paper also shows that the ad hoc regularization used to prevent those problems can itself produce unexpected failures.

Universal boosting variational inference changes the geometry of the optimization by using Hellinger distance. This prevents the degeneracy affecting other gradient-based approaches, avoids difficult joint optimization of a component and its weight, and simplifies reoptimizing mixture weights. The authors prove convergence to the best approximation available in the chosen mixture family for any target density and component family, including misspecified families.

A scalable implementation uses exponential-family components and standard stochastic optimization. The paper further connects Hellinger approximation error to errors in posterior probabilities, moments, and importance sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and models report reliable, accurate posterior approximations. The convergence guarantee concerns the best attainable mixture approximation, which need not equal the target when the family is misspecified.
neurips-2019-universal-boosting-variatio.tldr: UBVI uses Hellinger geometry to avoid degenerate mixture optimization and converge to the best approximation in the chosen mixture family.

paragraphs: A model trained across modalities such as images and language should capture what they share while retaining information specific to each. This paper turns that broad ambition into four criteria for successful multimodal generative learning. It then proposes a mixture-of-experts multimodal variational autoencoder, MMVAE, and evaluates it against those criteria.

The first criterion is an implicit separation of shared and private information in the latent representation. The next two concern generation: samples produced jointly across modalities should agree, and generation of one modality from another should also be coherent. The fourth asks whether combining modalities improves learning for the individual modalities themselves.

The authors study different modality combinations, including a challenging image-language dataset, and report qualitative and quantitative evidence that MMVAE meets all four criteria. This gives the evaluation several complementary targets: representation structure, agreement in jointly generated outputs, cross-modal generation, and benefits to individual modalities. The findings support the proposed model across those aspects in the settings examined.
neurips-2019-variational-mixture-of-expe.tldr: MMVAE meets four proposed criteria for multimodal learning, spanning shared representations, coherent generation, and improved individual-modality learning.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational model to investigate visual sequence-learning effects observed in primate visual cortex. The network learns by predicting incoming video, using the video itself as its teaching signal. Its training objective minimizes prediction errors at multiple levels, allowing a hierarchy of representations to develop through self-supervised learning.

The architecture combines fast feedforward processing through a sparsely convolutional deep network with feedback synthesis through stacked LSTM modules. Recurrent feedback leads lower-level population representations to form semantic clusters of global movement patterns. These representations help the network learn relationships among movements and support state-of-the-art long-range video prediction on the evaluated benchmarks.

Without additional tuning, the model also exhibits neurophysiological correlates of visual sequence memories observed in the early visual cortex of awake monkeys. This agreement suggests that learning through prediction may help explain cortical representation learning. The result connects a working video-prediction model with neural observations, supporting the proposed principle as a possible account of the observed sequence-learning effects.
neurips-2019-visual-sequence-learning-in.tldr: A hierarchical video-prediction network develops movement representations and reproduces observed neural correlates of visual sequence memory without further tuning.
